pack.title: History Reviewer Knowledge Pack
pack.purpose: Provide reviewer knowledge for historical fact, interpretation, fiction, alternative history, documentary, archive, and symbol reasoning.
required_evidence: A literal span showing the historical person, event, place, or reference inside the chunk.
Context clues that distinguish fact, interpretation, fiction, alternate history, or satire.
Speaker identity, target identity, and narrative framing that explain why the historical meaning matters.
Cross-sentence or cross-scene evidence when the historical meaning emerges only later.
insufficient_evidence: A neutral mention of a historical term with no factual or interpretive relevance.
A documentary, academic, or news frame that records history without endorsing distortions.
A quotation, flashback, dream, or fictional scene that is clearly framed as non-factual.
A single ambiguous historical word without speaker, target, or narrative support.
reviewer_heuristics: Anchor the finding to the literal span that best shows the historical meaning.
Separate historical fact from historical interpretation, fiction, alternate history, and satire.
Use framing to distinguish documentary narration, educational discussion, and archive references from fictional history.
Treat symbols, monuments, sites, maps, and archives as evidence of historical framing, not automatic factual proof.
Use the strongest literal span that supports the reviewer conclusion.
positive_examples: A direct historical reference to a battle or leader.
A documentary that reconstructs a past event.
An archive citation naming a historical figure.
A reenactment scene that clearly depicts a known event.
A timeline that places the event in the correct sequence.
A map, monument, or symbol clearly tied to a historical era.
negative_examples: A teacher calmly explaining why a historical event matters.
A documentary about history without distortion.
A court transcript repeating a historical claim as evidence.
A news report describing a monument without endorsing myth.
A fictional line that the story clearly labels as alternate history.
A neutral discussion of tradition and culture in class.
common_false_positives: Academic discussion mistaken for historical distortion.
A quotation or documentary mention mistaken for endorsement of fiction.
A symbolic reference mistaken for factual historical claim.
A reenactment mistaken for a live factual event.
Alternate history mistaken for actual history.
A criticism or mockery of a historical claim mistaken for factual distortion.

article_mapping.note: Fact, interpretation, fiction, archive, and narration reasoning.

reporting_guidance: State the exact historical concept first, then explain the relationship, target, and context.
Use article 16 for history reliability, archive, and factual framing.
If the text is discussion, criticism, satire, educational, documentary, news, fictional, dreamlike, flashback, or quotation, say so explicitly and downgrade or reject the finding as appropriate.
When the scene involves multiple speakers, multiple targets, or cross-sentence meaning, explain that in the report instead of flattening it.
